summary: Specifies extensions to the Host Identity Protocol for NAT traversal, using the ICE methodology to find a working path between two hosts and standard techniques to relay when needed. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5770 extends HIP so hosts behind NATs can try to communicate. They exchange possible addresses, test address pairs, and use relays when a direct path is not available.

subtitle: HIP extensions that use UDP, address candidates and relays to find paths through NATs.

tldr.problem: HIP runs directly over IP, which creates problems when a network address translator changes packet addresses. Hosts behind NATs may not be able to exchange HIP control or ESP data packets directly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC encapsulates HIP control and ESP packets in UDP, uses ICE connectivity checks to test candidate address pairs, and defines a HIP relay for control traffic and TURN relays for data when needed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5770 is Experimental. It defines a procedure that tries to find a working direct path and can use relays when a direct path is unavailable.

today: RFC 5770 is Experimental and is published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation. The RFC metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why HIP Needs NAT Traversal
sections.content:
HIP normally runs directly over IPv4 or IPv6 and coordinates IPsec ESP security associations. A NAT changes addresses as packets cross a network boundary, so HIP packets may not pass through it as expected.

The RFC uses techniques from Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE). Hosts gather candidate transport addresses, exchange them during the HIP base exchange and test address pairs to find a usable path.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP packets can fail when they meet a NAT that changes network addresses. These extensions let HIP hosts exchange possible addresses and test which pairs can communicate.

sections.title: Registering and Gathering Addresses
sections.content:
A host may register with a HIP relay server and learn the transport address the relay observes for it. It can gather host, server-reflexive and relayed candidates. Hosts negotiate whether to use UDP encapsulation alone or UDP with ICE connectivity checks.

The hosts also negotiate the minimum time between connectivity-check transactions. If neither host proposes a value, the minimum is 500 milliseconds. The RFC says hosts should not use values below 20 milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Before testing paths, a host can register with a relay and collect possible addresses. The hosts also agree how much time to leave between connectivity checks.

sections.title: Relays, Checks and Data Traffic
sections.content:
A HIP relay forwards HIP control packets between an Initiator and a Responder. It does not forward ESP data traffic; a TURN server can relay data when needed. The hosts first complete the HIP base exchange through the relay, then ICE checks candidate pairs and selects an operational pair for ESP traffic.

If the checks fail, the hosts must not send ESP traffic to each other, although they may continue HIP signaling over the base-exchange path. When a NAT mapping may expire during an idle period, an end host sends keepalives every 15 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The HIP relay helps the hosts exchange control messages, while a TURN server can carry data. ICE tests candidate pairs and selects one for data when a working pair is found.

sections.title: Privacy and Relay Risks
sections.content:
Locator addresses are sent in plain text. The RFC notes that sharing them can reveal a host's physical location or details about a private network. A host may omit some locators, but this can prevent a direct path and require a TURN relay.

The RFC also describes a replay risk for base exchanges through a relay when a responder is disconnected from it. It describes relay-inserted nonces, which hosts sign, as one protection against this attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing candidate addresses can reveal network or location information. The RFC also describes a replay attack against relay exchanges and a nonce-based protection.
